overview:
In October 1517 an Augustinian friar and university lecturer at Wittenberg circulated ninety-five propositions attacking the sale of indulgences — payments that promised remission of punishment for sin. Martin Luther meant to start an academic disputation in Latin; whether he ever nailed the sheet to the castle church door is a story historians treat with caution, since the earliest account comes secondhand and after his death. What is certain is that printers seized the text, translated and reprinted it within weeks, and that Luther followed it with a torrent of cheap German pamphlets. Behind the immediate quarrel lay older grievances: the reform demands of Jan Hus and John Wycliffe a century earlier, humanist scholarship that put the Greek New Testament against the Latin Vulgate, and long-standing German resentment of papal taxation. By the Diet of Worms in 1521 Luther had been excommunicated and outlawed, and protected by his own prince — the pattern that would define the next century, in which theology travelled inseparably from politics.

What followed was less a single movement than several, often hostile to one another. Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich and later John Calvin in Geneva built a Reformed tradition that broke with Luther over the eucharist and went much further in stripping churches of images; whitewashed walls and smashed statuary across Switzerland, the Netherlands and Scotland are among the most visible physical traces the period left. Anabaptists and other radicals rejected infant baptism and state churches altogether and were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. Peasants in southern Germany invoked the gospel in the rising of 1524–25 and were crushed, with Luther urging the princes on. In England the break with Rome began as Henry VIII's dynastic quarrel and only later acquired a doctrinal life of its own. Lutheranism became the state religion across Scandinavia; Reformed and Antitrinitarian churches flourished for a time in Poland-Lithuania, Hungary and Transylvania. Rome answered with its own reform — the Council of Trent, new orders such as the Jesuits, an Index of forbidden books — which historians now describe less as a mere reaction than as a parallel movement of discipline and renewal.

The settlements came through exhaustion rather than persuasion. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each German prince choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism for his own territory, a formula that bought decades but excluded Calvinists and left subjects no choice at all. France endured a generation of civil wars; the Dutch provinces fought free of Spain; and the Thirty Years' War from 1618 devastated central Europe before the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognised Calvinism alongside the other two and effectively conceded that Latin Christendom would not be reassembled. The end date of 1648 is a convention rather than a fact — some historians close the story at 1555, others extend a "long Reformation" well into the eighteenth century, arguing that the slow reshaping of ordinary belief and practice took far longer than the political settlements did.
significance: The Reformation permanently ended the idea of a single church in western Europe, and in doing so forced the invention of arrangements for living with religious difference — territorial toleration, then grudging coexistence, eventually the notion that a state's confession might be separable from its subjects' consciences. It bound rulers and churches together in what scholars call confessionalization, giving early modern states new reach into schooling, marriage, poor relief and moral discipline on both sides of the divide. It made vernacular scripture and vernacular argument central to European public life, and pushed literacy, print and polemic into a relationship that has been read ever since as a forerunner of modern mass media. Its rivalries were also exported: Catholic and Protestant missions carried competing versions of Christianity to the Americas, Africa and Asia, and confessional identity shaped colonial settlement from New England to Brazil. The denominational map of the Christian world today still largely follows the fault lines drawn between 1517 and 1648.
coverage: Written from general reference overviews — Britannica, Wikipedia, a museum essay on the Reformation and art — plus search summaries of scholarship on confessionalization and on women's experience of reform; this dataset holds no events at all beneath the story, so nothing here is anchored to a specific place or date on the map. The surviving record is heavily weighted toward the literate, male, and polemical: printed pamphlets, theologians' correspondence and court and inquisition records survive far better than what ordinary parishioners actually believed, and much of what we know about radicals such as the Anabaptists comes through the hands of the authorities who prosecuted them. Reformation history east of Germany and beyond Europe is thinner here than it should be, and the framing dates themselves are a scholarly convention rather than a settled boundary.
